Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, speaking in Parliament on Monday, said hundreds of thousands of care workers will be exempt from the hardline rules, offering a concession amid a political outcry within the governing Labour Party. Permanent residency, known in the UK as indefinite leave to remain, carries the right to work, study, use the free National Health Service and claim welfare benefits. Until now, it has been granted after five years. The new rules, set to take effect next year, tie eligibility for permanent residency to income. People who earn more than 50,000 pounds a year ($67,000) will still be able to apply after five years, and those earning more than 125,000 pounds ($167,500) after three. Everyone else will be placed on the 10-year path. The median salary in the UK is about 39,000 pounds (roughly $52,000). The rules will apply retroactively to workers already in the country. “Settlement should not be automatic. It should be earned,” Mahmood, the home secretary, told Parliament, adding that the changes would restore fairness by linking the right to settle to what immigrants contribute. “Those who contribute most will settle fastest,” she said. “Those who don’t play by the rules will be refused or wait longer.” The UK government first proposed last year that lower-skilled workers wait 10 to 15 years for permanent residency. But the plan drew fierce opposition from unions and parts of the Labour Party, particularly over its effect on care workers, who are often poorly paid and work in a sector that has long struggled to fill vacancies. Many of them arrived in the early 2020s, as the country was reeling from the COVID-19 pandemic, to fill gaps left by European workers who had departed after Brexit. clusters.text: New York governor says case is ‘devastating reminder of what’s at stake’ when vaccine protections are eroded A child in rural northern New York has died after contracting measles, marking the state’s first death from the disease in 30 years, state officials announced on Monday. The child died in Lewis county, about 93 miles (150km) north of Syracuse, New York governor Kathy Hochul said. “I am heartbroken to learn that a child in Lewis County has died after contracting measles,” Hochul said in a statement. Hochul linked the death to the federal government’s stance on immunisation, saying: “This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.” Measles is a highly contagious virus that can cause serious health complications. Although rare, deaths from measles occur in approximately one to three patients per 1,000 cases. The US stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed three measles-associated deaths in the US this year, but state health departments have reported higher numbers. Pennsylvania health officials have reported six deaths this year . Hochul declared a disaster emergency in early October because of measles cases in neighbouring states and in rural areas of New York. The executive order extended the pool of people who can administer measles vaccines to include paramedics, midwives and others, and it allowed nurses to join doctors in ordering testing. The CDC reported 4,588 cases of measles across the country in 2026 as of late October – more than double the tally for 2025. Pennsylvania alone reported 1,338 cases on the same day. The CDC also reported large outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah, both of which are reporting more than 500 cases. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US department of health and human services (HHS), has faced criticism for his comments on some vaccines, and made sweeping changes to vaccination policy, including cutting childhood immunisation recommendations by a third.

clusters.title: NASA's Swift Observatory to re-enter Earth's atmosphere
outlets: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
clusters.text: LOS ANGELES, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is expected to re-enter Earth's atmosphere on Wednesday, nearly 22 years after its launch, NASA said in a statement on Monday. Launched in 2004, Swift was the first-of-its-kind multiwavelength observatory designed to study gamma-ray bursts, some of the universe's most powerful explosions, using its three telescopes. As of Monday, the U.S. Space Force predicted that the roughly 3,200-pound (1,450-kilogram) spacecraft would re-enter the atmosphere at around 3:30 a.m. Eastern Time (0830 GMT) Wednesday, with an uncertainty window of 11 hours. NASA expects most of the spacecraft to burn up as it travels through the atmosphere, but some components are expected to survive re-entry. Depending on the timing of re-entry, any surviving debris could land in areas between 20.6 degrees south and 20.6 degrees north, while the risk of harm to anyone on Earth is very low, estimated at approximately one in 2,100, according to NASA. NASA had sought to extend Swift's operational life through a commercial spacecraft servicing mission, but the effort was scaled back to technology demonstrations after the servicing spacecraft encountered technical problems and ran low on fuel. NASA said on Oct. 23 that Swift had ended its science mission as its orbit continued to decay. Originally designed for a two-year prime mission, Swift went on to operate for more than two decades, serving as a multi-tool for exploring the universe, observing a wide range of light, rapidly pointing at short-lived outbursts, and sending alerts to other facilities to help coordinate follow-up observations, according to NASA. ■

clusters.text: Google says one of its Android manufacturing partners secretly built a backdoor in 1.3 million devices and turned them into a botnet. The company says it has now dismantled the backdoor and “cut ties” with the manufacturer, the Shenzhen, China-based Videostrong Technology Co., which has been banned from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software for them. The infected devices were used without owners’ knowledge for “malicious activity,” like ad fraud, data exfiltration, and routing unauthorized network traffic. Google claims the “backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain,” saying: > Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices. It wasn’t just one device that was impacted, either — the malware was found “built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years.” Most of those were Android TV set-top boxes, but the botnet also infected other “Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.” Google says Videostrong used “obfuscation techniques” to load the malware onto users’ devices after they booted up the hardware for the first time. Google also says it made changes to its review process for device manufacturers after this incident.

clusters.text: The first ODI between India and Sri Lanka is all set to be moved out of the Arun Jaitley Stadium in New Delhi. The Delhi and District Cricket Association (DDCA) has requested the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) to shift the December 13 game out of the national capital. According to sources, the DDCA is believed to have written to the BCCI, citing its inability to host the match on the scheduled date. The association is believed to have cited multiple reasons for the request, including the pollution levels in Delhi at this time of the year. The stadium, of course, is also undergoing renovation. Sources have revealed that the DDCA is concerned about the poor air quality in the capital, which is notorious for its high AQI levels. Last December, the capital recorded an average AQI of 351, with similar levels recorded on Monday (November 2). The DDCA wants to be safe rather than sorry, given its past experience. “More than the renovation work, we want the match to be moved because of AQI in Delhi,” a source familiar with the development told Cricbuzz. During a Test match between India and Sri Lanka in December 2017, some Sri Lankan players were seen throwing up on the ground. DDCA sources say they do not want a repeat of that fracas. The association is believed to have asked for another game sometime next year. This match was supposed to be the first of the three matches in the ODI series, with the other two scheduled to be played in Bengaluru on December 16 and Ahmedabad on December 19. The BCCI will now have to rejig the schedule of the series. The BCCI had previously dismissed reports that the match was being moved out, with secretary Devajit Saikia categorically denying plans to shift the game. “Reports suggesting that the India-Sri Lanka ODI match scheduled in Delhi may be shifted to Ahmedabad are not accurate. There has been no such decision by the BCCI. We request media colleagues to kindly refer to official BCCI communications for any updates regarding the schedule. Further, it needs to be reiterated that bilateral matches are primarily allotted by following a standard policy," Saikia had said on October 12. With the DDCA itself requesting the BCCI to move the match, the board may have little option but to relocate the game.

clusters.text: Hospitals, nursing homes and clinics in Ranchi have been given seven days to display their registration certificates, service charges, doctors’ credentials and other essential information for patients under an order issued by the Office of the Civil Surgeon-cum-Chief Medical Officer. The office order, dated October 29, 2026, directs applicable clinical establishments across Ranchi district to comply with the Clinical Establishments Act (CEA) guidelines and maintain compliance on a continuous basis. The directive follows a request received through official email from social activist Jyoti Sharma regarding compliance with the guidelines. The order identifies six categories of information that must be displayed prominently at healthcare facilities. Six categories of information to be displayed Under the order, healthcare establishments must meet the following requirements: Registration certificate: Display a valid and updated registration certificate or licence issued by the competent authority at the reception or another conspicuous location accessible to patients and the public. Service charges: Display an updated, itemised rate chart covering consultation fees, investigation charges, procedure charges, bed charges and other applicable fees. Doctors’ credentials: Clearly display doctors’ names, medical qualifications, registration details with the relevant medical council, specialities and consultation or duty timings. Available services: Provide information about the medical services and facilities available at the establishment. Patient information: Display information on patient rights, grievance-redressal mechanisms and other particulars required under applicable rules and guidelines. Transparency in billing: Ensure transparency in charges for medical services and do not impose undisclosed charges contrary to applicable rules and regulations. Compliance required within seven days The order directs all concerned establishments to comply within seven days of its issuance and maintain compliance thereafter.
